Stage 3 · Language

Opening, carrying on, and reacting

A story only works if two people are doing the work.

Read this exchange.
  • A: I heard this incredible story about a woman who lost her wedding ring…
  • B: What happened?
  • A: You’re not going to believe this, but she was digging up carrots…
  • B: No way! That’s incredible!
What is B actually doing in this conversation?
Telling a story in conversation is a two-person activity, and English has fixed phrases for both roles.

You can have perfect narrative tenses and still fail to hold a listener. What makes a spoken story work in English is a layer of fixed phrases that carry almost no information but do essential social work: they claim the floor, promise that the story is worth hearing, mark the turning point, and signal the end.

The teller needs four kinds of phrase. An opener that announces a story is coming, so nobody interrupts (You’ll never believe what happened…). A scene-setter, almost always in the past continuous (So I was walking home at about ten when…). Sequencers that keep the events flowing (So then… The next thing I knew…). And a closing line that hands the floor back (Anyway, that’s why I never take the cable car).

The listener has a role that is not optional. In English-speaking cultures, a listener who says nothing throughout a story is read as uninterested. Short response tokens — Really? No way! You’re joking! Go on! What happened next? — tell the teller that the story is landing and should continue. This is a genuine cross-cultural difference, and learners who stay silent out of politeness often produce exactly the opposite effect from the one they intend.

Intonation carries much of the meaning here. Really? said with a rising tone means ‘tell me more’; the same word with a falling tone sounds bored or sarcastic. Suspense, likewise, is created by pausing before the key word, not by speaking louder.

Before you look at the table: the table below lists the phrases by the job they do rather than by meaning, because their meaning is almost entirely functional. Learn each one as a fixed whole; they do not change form.
Who says what, and when
MomentThe teller saysThe listener says
OpeningI’ll never forget the day… · That reminds me of… · I heard this incredible story about…Really? · Go on. · What happened?
Building upSo then… · Anyway,… · Meanwhile,…Oh no, that’s awful. · What happened next?
The big momentYou’re not going to believe this, but… · And suddenly…You’re joking. · What, you mean…?!
FinishingIn the end… · It turned out that…No way! · That’s incredible!

The reaction is not politeness, it is fuel. Without Really? and What happened next? the teller runs out of energy and cuts the story short. Two reactions per minute is the minimum.

“You’re not going to believe this, but…” is a signal, not a sentence. It tells the listener that the surprising part is arriving, so they can get ready to react.

Watch the delivery. These phrases only work with the right voice. No way! said flatly sounds bored; the voice has to go up. If you are not sure, record yourself and listen back.

Say vs tell. You tell somebody something; you say something to somebody. Not He said me the story, but He told me the story.

Full grammar reference — telling a story so people listen — and reacting to one

What it is

Storytelling in conversation is a two-person activity. The teller uses a set of fixed openers, sequencers and dramatic devices to keep attention; the listener uses short response tokens to show they are still there and want more. Neither set is optional in natural English: a story told without them sounds like a report, and a story received in silence stalls.

What it means, and what it does

These phrases carry almost no information — their job is social. You’ll never believe what happened tells the listener nothing about the events, but it buys the teller the floor and promises that the story is worth the wait. Go on! tells the teller that the listener is engaged and the story should continue. This is why B1 learners who know all the past tenses can still fail to hold a listener.

When and why we use it

You can have perfect narrative tenses and still fail to hold a listener. What makes a spoken story work in English is a layer of fixed phrases that carry almost no information but do essential social work: they claim the floor, promise that the story is worth hearing, mark the turning point, and signal the end.

The teller needs four kinds of phrase. An opener that announces a story is coming, so nobody interrupts (You’ll never believe what happened…). A scene-setter, almost always in the past continuous (So I was walking home at about ten when…). Sequencers that keep the events flowing (So then… The next thing I knew…). And a closing line that hands the floor back (Anyway, that’s why I never take the cable car).

The listener has a role that is not optional. In English-speaking cultures, a listener who says nothing throughout a story is read as uninterested. Short response tokens — Really? No way! You’re joking! Go on! What happened next? — tell the teller that the story is landing and should continue. This is a genuine cross-cultural difference, and learners who stay silent out of politeness often produce exactly the opposite effect from the one they intend.

Intonation carries much of the meaning here. Really? said with a rising tone means ‘tell me more’; the same word with a falling tone sounds bored or sarcastic. Suspense, likewise, is created by pausing before the key word, not by speaking louder.

Typical situations

This language belongs to any informal conversation: telling a colleague what happened at the weekend, recounting something that went wrong, sharing news, or listening while somebody else does the same.

  • Claiming the floor — announcing that a story is coming, so nobody interrupts.You’ll never believe what happened to me yesterday.
  • Setting the scene — time and place first, in the past continuous, before any event.So I was walking home at about ten when…
  • Moving on — short sequencers that keep the events flowing.So then he turned round, and after that everything went dark.
  • Building suspense — slowing down just before the key event.And then, suddenly, I realized I was underwater.
  • Showing you are listening — short tokens, usually with rising intonation.Really? · No way! · What happened next?
  • Reacting to the point — a fuller response once the story lands.That’s incredible! · You’re joking!
  • Closing the story — a line that signals the end and hands the floor back.And that was that. · Anyway, that’s why I never take the cable car.

How it differs from similar structures

Really? (neutral, keeps the story going) · No way! (strong surprise, informal) · That’s incredible. (a full evaluation, usually at the end, not in the middle).
What happened next? asks for the following event · What happened in the end? asks you to skip to the outcome. They are not interchangeable.

How to build it

Opener: You’ll never believe + what / who / where + clause
Scene: So I was + verb-ing + when + past simple event
Sequencer: So then / And after that / The next thing I knew, + clause
Response token: Really? / No way! / Go on! / What happened next?
OpenerYou’ll never believe what happened. — note the statement word order after what.
Scene settingI was standing at the bus stop when a car pulled up.
SequencingSo then… · After that… · The next thing I knew…
SuspenseAnd suddenly… · All of a sudden… · Out of nowhere…
Short responseReally? · Seriously? · No way! · You’re joking!
Asking for moreWhat happened next? · And then what? · Go on!
ClosingAnd that was that. · Anyway, that’s the story.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • Response tokens live or die on intonation. Really? with a rising tone means ‘tell me more’; with a falling tone it sounds bored or sarcastic.
  • No way! and You’re joking! carry a wide pitch fall from a high start. Said flat, they sound like disbelief in the unfriendly sense.
  • Suspense is created by pausing before the key word, not by speaking louder: and then — suddenly — the lights went out.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • You’ll never believe what happened keeps statement word order after what: not what did happen. This is an embedded question, and it behaves like the reported questions in Lesson 35.
  • Guess what! is an even shorter opener and expects the listener to say What? before you continue.
  • Response tokens are not interruptions. A listener who says nothing for a whole story is read as uninterested in English-speaking cultures, which is a genuine cross-cultural difference worth naming.
  • Overuse flattens the effect. One opener, two or three sequencers and one suspense marker is enough for a two-minute story.
  • Anyway is the standard signal that you are closing a story or returning to an earlier topic. It is not rude.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • You’ll never believe what did happen. → You’ll never believe what happened.After what in an embedded clause, keep statement word order.
  • So then suddenly I was falling into the stream and I was breaking my leg. → So then, suddenly, I fell into the stream and broke my leg.Single completed events take the past simple, not the continuous.
  • Tell me the story! Go on the story. → Go on! What happened next?Go on! is fixed and takes no object.
  • It is incredible! → That’s incredible!The reaction refers back to what was said, so English uses that.
  • I will tell you what happened yesterday, listen. → You’ll never believe what happened yesterday.Use the fixed opener; the literal version sounds like an announcement, not a story.
  • At the end, that’s why I never go there. → Anyway, that’s why I never go there.Anyway is the closing signal; at the end refers to a place.

More examples in context

  • openerYou’ll never believe who I ran into this morning.
  • sceneSo I was queuing for coffee when someone tapped me on the shoulder.
  • sequencerSo then she asked me for my number.
  • sequencerThe next thing I knew, we were talking about school.
  • suspenseAnd then, suddenly, I remembered where I’d seen her before.
  • listenerNo way! Seriously?
  • listenerGo on — what happened next?
  • listenerYou’re joking! After all that time?
  • evaluationThat’s incredible. What are the chances?
  • closingAnyway, that’s how we ended up meeting again after ten years.

A tip for remembering it

Rehearse a story as four beats: hook (You’ll never believe…), scene (I was …-ing when…), turn (And then suddenly…), close (Anyway, that’s why…). When you are the listener, aim to say something every three or four sentences — a single word is enough.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Storytelling needs fixed phrases, not just correct tenses.
  2. Open with a hook, set the scene in the past continuous, then move with so then / after that.
  3. Build suspense with a pause and suddenly, not with volume.
  4. Keep statement word order after what: you’ll never believe what happened.
  5. As the listener, react every few sentences: Really? No way! Go on!
  6. Close with Anyway,… to hand the floor back.

Stage 5 · Main input

The same story, written down

Read it as a writer. You are going to write one like it.

Before you read: a woman loses her wedding ring in 1995 and finds it again ten years later.

Guess first. Then read and see.

The ring that came back

I’ll never forget the day my grandmother lost her wedding ring.

It was an ordinary Tuesday in 1995. She had been baking all morning, and while she was working the dough she suddenly noticed that her hand felt light. The ring was gone.

We looked everywhere. My grandfather even took up part of the kitchen floor, board by board. As soon as one of us gave up, another one started again. By the end of the week we had searched the whole house twice, and we had found nothing.

Ten years later, on a cold morning in the garden, she was digging up carrots for soup. She pulled one out, looked at it, and stopped. The carrot had grown straight through a small gold circle.

You’re not going to believe this, but it was the ring. It had been lying in the soil since the day she lost it, and the carrot had simply grown through the middle of it.

She wears it again now. Remarkably, it still fits. And whenever anybody in our family loses something, she says the same thing: don’t look for it. Plant something and wait.

What the model does, in five moves
  • One opening line that promises a story and stops.
  • An ordinary scene first, so the strange part has something to break.
  • What everybody did — and why it did not work.
  • The surprise, signalled one sentence before it lands.
  • Where it stands now, in two or three lines. Then stop.
